perforate

PUR-fuh-rayt · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To perforate is to pierce and make holes in something, often in a row or pattern.

The postage stamps are perforated so they can be torn apart cleanly along the sheet.

Example

Years of exposure to acidic rain had begun to perforate the old iron gate with rust holes.

The rust didn't just discolor the gate -- it ate straight through it in spots, leaving actual holes, which is exactly perforate.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

puncture: To puncture is to make one small hole with a sharp point -- a nail punctures a tire, a needle punctures a seal. To perforate is to riddle a surface with holes, usually a whole row or pattern of them, so one careful poke is a puncture, not a perforation.

pierce: To pierce is to drive something sharp into or clean through -- one act, one hole: an arrow pierces a shield. To perforate multiplies that into many holes across a surface, often in a deliberate row or pattern. Pierce describes the single stab; perforate describes the peppered result.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

seal: close something completely so nothing can pass through

Where it sits · how far the damage spreads

prick → perforate → shatter

prick vs. perforate: A prick is one tiny hole from a fine point; perforate usually means a whole row or pattern of holes.

shatter vs. perforate: Perforate leaves an object full of holes but still whole; shatter breaks it apart entirely.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — per-: through (Latin)

root — for: to bore or pierce (Latin forare)

suffix — -ate: verb-forming ending (Latin -atus)

Put it together: Perforate comes from Latin per- ('through') + forare ('to bore or pierce') + -ate -- literally 'to bore through.'

Where it comes from: Latin forare meant 'to bore or pierce,' so something perforated has quite literally been bored through -- picture the neat line of punched holes that lets a sheet tear cleanly. The root forare left almost no other common English words behind, so this one carries it nearly alone.

Strength Check

Word Choice

Perforate is often used for an intentional, useful pattern of holes (a stamp sheet, a coupon) as well as accidental damage (rust, an ulcer perforating tissue).
